questions.question_text: Given below are two statements : Given : Molar mass of $C,H,O,Cl$ are $12,1,16$ and $35.5gmol^{-1}$ , respectively Statement I : In $30%(w/w)$ solution of methanol in $CCl_{4}($ at T K $)$ , the mole fraction of $CCl_{4}$ is equal to 0.33 . Statement II : Mixture of methanol and $CCl_{4}$ shows positive deviation from Raoult's law. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.question_html:
Given below are two statements :

Given : Molar mass of $C,H,O,Cl$ are $12,1,16$ and $35.5gmol^{-1}$ , respectively

Statement I : In $30%(w/w)$ solution of methanol in $CCl_{4}($ at T K $)$ , the mole fraction of $CCl_{4}$ is equal to 0.33 .

Statement II : Mixture of methanol and $CCl_{4}$ shows positive deviation from Raoult's law. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
options.html: Both Statement I and Statement II are true

options.label: B
options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
options.html: Both Statement I and Statement II are false

options.label: C
options.text: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
options.html: Statement I is true but Statement II is false

options.label: D
options.text: Statement I is false but Statement II is true
options.html: Statement I is false but Statement II is true

questions.explanation_text: Molar masses: C = 12 g mol⁻¹ H = 1 g mol⁻¹ O = 16 g mol⁻¹ Cl = 35.5 g mol⁻¹ Formula masses: For methanol, CH₃OH: $M=12+(3 \times 1)+16+1=32\text{g mol}^{-1}$ For carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄: $M=12+(4 \times 35.5)=12+142=154\text{g mol}^{-1}$ This means in 100 g of solution : Mass of methanol = 30 g Mass of CCl₄ = 70 g $n_{\text{methanol}}=\frac{30}{32}=0.9375\text{mol}$ $n_{\text{CCl}_{4}}=\frac{70}{154}=0.4545\text{mol}$ Total moles = $0.9375+0.4545=1.392$ So, $x_{\text{methanol}}=\frac{0.9375}{1.392}=0.674$ $x_{\text{CCl}_{4}}=\frac{0.4545}{1.392}=0.326 \approx 0.33$ Hence, Statement I is correct. Methanol is polar and forms hydrogen bonds. Carbon tetrachloride is non-polar. When they are mixed, the H-bonding between methanol molecules weakens (since CCl₄ cannot form hydrogen bonds with methanol). → The intermolecular attraction between unlike molecules decreases. As a result, the escaping tendency of molecules increases and vapour pressure increases , leading to positive deviation from Raoult’s law. Hence, Statement II is also correct. Final Answer Both Statement I and Statement II are true. $\text{Option A}$
questions.explanation_html:
• Molar masses:

  • C = 12 g mol⁻¹

  • H = 1 g mol⁻¹

  • O = 16 g mol⁻¹

  • Cl = 35.5 g mol⁻¹

Formula masses:

  • For methanol, CH₃OH:

    $M=12+(3 \times 1)+16+1=32\text{g mol}^{-1}$

  • For carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄:

    $M=12+(4 \times 35.5)=12+142=154\text{g mol}^{-1}$

This means in 100 g of solution:

  • Mass of methanol = 30 g

  • Mass of CCl₄ = 70 g

$n_{\text{methanol}}=\frac{30}{32}=0.9375\text{mol}$

$n_{\text{CCl}_{4}}=\frac{70}{154}=0.4545\text{mol}$

Total moles = $0.9375+0.4545=1.392$

So,

$x_{\text{methanol}}=\frac{0.9375}{1.392}=0.674$

$x_{\text{CCl}_{4}}=\frac{0.4545}{1.392}=0.326 \approx 0.33$

Hence, Statement I is correct.

  • Methanol is polar and forms hydrogen bonds.

  • Carbon tetrachloride is non-polar.

  • When they are mixed, the H-bonding between methanol molecules weakens (since CCl₄ cannot form hydrogen bonds with methanol).

    → The intermolecular attraction between unlike molecules decreases.

As a result, the escaping tendency of molecules increases and vapour pressure increases, leading to positive deviation from Raoult’s law.

Hence, Statement II is also correct.

Final Answer

Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

$\text{Option A}$

questions.question_text: At $27^{\circ}C,0.1M,1LK_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]$ aqueous solution and $0.1M,1LFeCl_{3}$ aqueous solution are placed in a container separated by a semi permeable membrane AB . Assume complete dissociation of both the solutes. Which of the following statement is correct?
questions.question_html: At $27^{\circ}C,0.1M,1LK_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]$ aqueous solution and $0.1M,1LFeCl_{3}$ aqueous solution are placed in a container separated by a semi permeable membrane AB . Assume complete dissociation of both the solutes. Which of the following statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Blue color is formed on both sides.
options.html: Blue color is formed on both sides.

options.label: B
options.text: Ionic solutes in aqueous solution can pass through semi-permeable membrane.
options.html: Ionic solutes in aqueous solution can pass through semi-permeable membrane.

options.label: C
options.text: Solution on side ' y ' is hypotonic.
options.html: Solution on side ' y ' is hypotonic.

options.label: D
options.text: To cause the reverse flow of solvent during osmosis, external pressure (any value) should be applied to side ' $x$ '.
options.html: To cause the reverse flow of solvent during osmosis, external pressure (any value) should be applied to side ' $x$ '.

questions.explanation_text: (A) A semi-permeable membrane (SPM) allows only solvent molecules (water) to pass through it. It does not allow ions to pass. So, the solute ions from the two sides cannot come together. Therefore, no blue colour (due to mixing of ions) will appear on either side. (B) Because ions cannot cross the SPM, only solvent molecules can move from one side to the other depending on osmotic pressure. (C) A hypotonic solution is the one which has lower osmotic pressure (lower “effective” concentration of solute particles). We use the NCERT relation for osmotic pressure: As osmotic pressure $(\pi)=iCRT$ $\begin{aligned} & K_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}] \longrightarrow 4K^{+}+Fe(CN)_{6}^{-4}( \because i=5) \\ & FeCl_{3} \longrightarrow Fe^{+3}+3Cl^{-}( \because i=4) \\ & \text{for side}x:\pi=5CRT=0.5RT( \because c=0.1m) \\ & y:\pi=0.4RT( \because c=0.1m) \end{aligned}$ effective concentration of $x=\overset{˙}{i} \times C=0.5M$ $y=i \times C=0.4m$ Since, effective concentration of $y$ is less than $x$ . Hence, $y$ is hypotonic. (D) In reverse osmosis, pressure is applied on the side having higher osmotic pressure (here, side $x$ ). But this applied external pressure must be greater than the osmotic pressure difference between the two sides. i.e. P applied > $(\pi_{x}-\pi_{y})$
questions.explanation_html:
(A) A semi-permeable membrane (SPM) allows only solvent molecules (water) to pass through it. It does not allow ions to pass.

So, the solute ions from the two sides cannot come together. Therefore, no blue colour (due to mixing of ions) will appear on either side.

(B) Because ions cannot cross the SPM, only solvent molecules can move from one side to the other depending on osmotic pressure.

(C) A hypotonic solution is the one which has lower osmotic pressure (lower “effective” concentration of solute particles).

We use the NCERT relation for osmotic pressure:

As osmotic pressure $(\pi)=iCRT$

$\begin{aligned} & K_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}] \longrightarrow 4K^{+}+Fe(CN)_{6}^{-4}( \because i=5) \\ & FeCl_{3} \longrightarrow Fe^{+3}+3Cl^{-}( \because i=4) \\ & \text{for side}x:\pi=5CRT=0.5RT( \because c=0.1m) \\ & y:\pi=0.4RT( \because c=0.1m) \end{aligned}$

effective concentration of $x=\overset{˙}{i} \times C=0.5M$

$y=i \times C=0.4m$

Since, effective concentration of $y$ is less than $x$ . Hence, $y$ is hypotonic.

(D) In reverse osmosis, pressure is applied on the side having higher osmotic pressure (here, side $x$ ). But this applied external pressure must be greater than the osmotic pressure difference between the two sides.

i.e. P applied > $(\pi_{x}-\pi_{y})$

questions.question_text: At $T(K),2$ moles of liquid A and 3 moles of liquid B are mixed. The vapour pressure of ideal solution formed is 320 mm Hg . At this stage, one mole of A and one mole of B are added to the solution. The vapour pressure is now measured as 328.6 mm Hg . The vapour pressure (in mm Hg ) of A and B are respectively:
questions.question_html: At $T(K),2$ moles of liquid A and 3 moles of liquid B are mixed. The vapour pressure of ideal solution formed is 320 mm Hg . At this stage, one mole of A and one mole of B are added to the solution. The vapour pressure is now measured as 328.6 mm Hg . The vapour pressure (in mm Hg ) of A and B are respectively:
questions.explanation_text: For an ideal solution, by Raoult’s law: $P_{\text{total}}=x_{A}P_{A}^{0}+x_{B}P_{B}^{0}$ where $P_{A}^{0},P_{B}^{0}$ are vapour pressures of pure liquids A and B. Step 1: First mixture (2 mol A + 3 mol B) Total moles $=2+3=5$ $x_{A}=\frac{2}{5},x_{B}=\frac{3}{5}$ Given $P_{\text{total}}=320$ mm Hg: $320=\frac{2}{5}P_{A}^{0}+\frac{3}{5}P_{B}^{0}$ Multiply by 5: $1600=2P_{A}^{0}+3P_{B}^{0}...(1)$ Step 2: After adding 1 mol A and 1 mol B New moles: A $=3$ , B $=4$ , total $=7$ $x_{A}=\frac{3}{7},x_{B}=\frac{4}{7}$ Given new vapour pressure $=328.6$ mm Hg: $328.6=\frac{3}{7}P_{A}^{0}+\frac{4}{7}P_{B}^{0}$ Multiply by 7: $2300.2=3P_{A}^{0}+4P_{B}^{0}...(2)$ Step 3: Solve the two equations From (1): $2P_{A}^{0}+3P_{B}^{0}=1600$ From (2): $3P_{A}^{0}+4P_{B}^{0}=2300.2$ Multiply (1) by 3: $6P_{A}^{0}+9P_{B}^{0}=4800$ Multiply (2) by 2: $6P_{A}^{0}+8P_{B}^{0}=4600.4$ Subtract: $P_{B}^{0}=4800-4600.4=199.6 \approx 200$ Put in (1): $2P_{A}^{0}+3(199.6)=1600$ $2P_{A}^{0}+598.8=1600$ $2P_{A}^{0}=1001.2 \Rightarrow P_{A}^{0}=500.6 \approx 500$ Final Answer Vapour pressures of A and B are approximately: $P_{A}^{0}=500\text{mm Hg},P_{B}^{0}=200\text{mm Hg}$ Correct option: C (500, 200)
questions.explanation_html:
For an ideal solution, by Raoult’s law:

$P_{\text{total}}=x_{A}P_{A}^{0}+x_{B}P_{B}^{0}$

where $P_{A}^{0},P_{B}^{0}$ are vapour pressures of pure liquids A and B.

Step 1: First mixture (2 mol A + 3 mol B)

Total moles $=2+3=5$

$x_{A}=\frac{2}{5},x_{B}=\frac{3}{5}$

Given $P_{\text{total}}=320$ mm Hg:

$320=\frac{2}{5}P_{A}^{0}+\frac{3}{5}P_{B}^{0}$

Multiply by 5:

$1600=2P_{A}^{0}+3P_{B}^{0}...(1)$

Step 2: After adding 1 mol A and 1 mol B

New moles: A $=3$ , B $=4$ , total $=7$

$x_{A}=\frac{3}{7},x_{B}=\frac{4}{7}$

Given new vapour pressure $=328.6$ mm Hg:

$328.6=\frac{3}{7}P_{A}^{0}+\frac{4}{7}P_{B}^{0}$

Multiply by 7:

$2300.2=3P_{A}^{0}+4P_{B}^{0}...(2)$

Step 3: Solve the two equations

From (1): $2P_{A}^{0}+3P_{B}^{0}=1600$

From (2): $3P_{A}^{0}+4P_{B}^{0}=2300.2$

Multiply (1) by 3:

$6P_{A}^{0}+9P_{B}^{0}=4800$

Multiply (2) by 2:

$6P_{A}^{0}+8P_{B}^{0}=4600.4$

Subtract:

$P_{B}^{0}=4800-4600.4=199.6 \approx 200$

Put in (1):

$2P_{A}^{0}+3(199.6)=1600$

$2P_{A}^{0}+598.8=1600$

$2P_{A}^{0}=1001.2 \Rightarrow P_{A}^{0}=500.6 \approx 500$

Final Answer

Vapour pressures of A and B are approximately:

$P_{A}^{0}=500\text{mm Hg},P_{B}^{0}=200\text{mm Hg}$

Correct option: C (500, 200)

questions.question_text: ' W ' g of a non-volatile electrolyte solid solute of molar mass ' M ' $gmol^{-1}$ when dissolved in 100 mL water, decreases vapour pressure of water from 640 mm Hg to 600 mm Hg . If aqueous solution of the electrolyte boils at 375 K and $K_{b}$ for water is $0.52Kkgmol^{-1}$ , then the mole fraction of the electrolyte solute $(x_{2})$ in the solution can be expressed as (Given : density of water $=1g/mL$ and boiling point of water $=373K$ )
questions.question_html:
' W ' g of a non-volatile electrolyte solid solute of molar mass ' M ' $gmol^{-1}$ when dissolved in 100 mL water, decreases vapour pressure of water from 640 mm Hg to 600 mm Hg . If aqueous solution of the electrolyte boils at 375 K and $K_{b}$ for water is $0.52Kkgmol^{-1}$ , then the mole fraction of the electrolyte solute $(x_{2})$ in the solution can be expressed as

(Given : density of water $=1g/mL$ and boiling point of water $=373K$ )
questions.explanation_text: Boiling point elevation: $\Delta T_{b}=375-373=2\text{K}$ Mass of water $=100\text{mL} \times 1\text{g mL}^{-1}=100\text{g}=0.1\text{kg}$ Molality: $m=\frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{kg of solvent}}=\frac{(W/M)}{0.1}=10\frac{W}{M}$ For electrolyte (NCERT): $\Delta T_{b}=iK_{b}m$ $2=i(0.52)(10\frac{W}{M})=i(5.2\frac{W}{M})$ $i=\frac{2}{5.2} \cdot \frac{M}{W}=\frac{5}{13} \cdot \frac{M}{W}$ Vapour pressure lowering: $\frac{\Delta p}{p^{\circ}}=\frac{640-600}{640}=\frac{40}{640}=\frac{1}{16}$ For electrolyte (NCERT): $\frac{\Delta p}{p^{\circ}}=ix_{2}$ So, $x_{2}=\frac{1/16}{i}=\frac{1}{16} \cdot \frac{1}{(\frac{5}{13} \cdot \frac{M}{W})}=\frac{1}{16} \cdot \frac{13}{5} \cdot \frac{W}{M}=\frac{13}{80} \cdot \frac{W}{M}$ $x_{2}=(\frac{1.3}{8})\frac{W}{M}$ Correct option: D
questions.explanation_html:
Boiling point elevation:

$\Delta T_{b}=375-373=2\text{K}$

Mass of water $=100\text{mL} \times 1\text{g mL}^{-1}=100\text{g}=0.1\text{kg}$

Molality:

$m=\frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{kg of solvent}}=\frac{(W/M)}{0.1}=10\frac{W}{M}$

For electrolyte (NCERT):

$\Delta T_{b}=iK_{b}m$

$2=i(0.52)(10\frac{W}{M})=i(5.2\frac{W}{M})$

$i=\frac{2}{5.2} \cdot \frac{M}{W}=\frac{5}{13} \cdot \frac{M}{W}$

Vapour pressure lowering:

$\frac{\Delta p}{p^{\circ}}=\frac{640-600}{640}=\frac{40}{640}=\frac{1}{16}$

For electrolyte (NCERT):

$\frac{\Delta p}{p^{\circ}}=ix_{2}$

So,

$x_{2}=\frac{1/16}{i}=\frac{1}{16} \cdot \frac{1}{(\frac{5}{13} \cdot \frac{M}{W})}=\frac{1}{16} \cdot \frac{13}{5} \cdot \frac{W}{M}=\frac{13}{80} \cdot \frac{W}{M}$

$x_{2}=(\frac{1.3}{8})\frac{W}{M}$

Correct option: D

Given below are two statements :

Statement I : The Henry's law constant $K_{H}$ is constant with respect to variations in solution's concentration over the range for which the solution is ideally dilute.

Statement II : $K_{H}$ does not differ for the same solute in different solvents.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.label: A

options.html: Both Statement I and Statement II are true

options.label: B
options.text: Statement I is true but Statement II is false

questions.explanation_text: Statement I: True. For an ideally dilute solution , Henry’s law is obeyed: $p=K_{H}x$ At a fixed temperature , $K_{H}$ remains constant over the concentration range where the solution behaves ideally (i.e., dilute enough). Statement II: False. $K_{H}$ depends on the nature of the gas (solute) and also the nature of the solvent (and temperature). So, for the same solute , $K_{H}$ can be different in different solvents . Correct option: B (Statement I is true but Statement II is false).

Statement II: False.

$K_{H}$ depends on the nature of the gas (solute) and also the nature of the solvent (and temperature). So, for the same solute, $K_{H}$ can be different in different solvents.

Correct option: B (Statement I is true but Statement II is false).

questions.question_text: The osmotic pressure of a living cell is 12 atm at 300 K. The strength of sodium chloride solution that is isotonic with the living cell at this temperature is ________ g L -1 . (Nearest integer) Given : R = 0.08 L atm K -1 mol -1 Assume complete dissociation of NaCl (Given: Molar mass of Na and Cl are 23 and 35.5 g mol -1 respectively.)
questions.question_html:
The osmotic pressure of a living cell is 12 atm at 300 K. The strength of sodium chloride solution that is isotonic with the living cell at this temperature is ________ g L-1. (Nearest integer)

Given : R = 0.08 L atm K-1 mol-1

Assume complete dissociation of NaCl

(Given: Molar mass of Na and Cl are 23 and 35.5 g mol-1 respectively.)
questions.explanation_text: Osmotic pressure ( $\pi$ ) = $12\text{atm}$ Temperature ( $T$ ) = $300\text{K}$ Gas constant ( $R$ ) = $0.08\text{L atm K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$ Sodium chloride (NaCl) is an electrolyte that breaks into ions in an aqueous solution: $\text{NaCl} \rightarrow \text{Na}^{+}+\text{Cl}^{-}$ Since it is given to assume complete dissociation, one unit of NaCl produces 2 ions. Therefore, the van 't Hoff factor, $i=2$ . According to the formula for osmotic pressure: $\pi=iCRT$ Substitute the given values into the equation: $12=2 \times C \times 0.08 \times 300$ $12=2 \times 24 \times C$ $12=48 \times C$ $C=\frac{12}{48}$ $C=0.25\text{mol L}^{-1}$ Molar mass of NaCl = Molar mass of Na + Molar mass of Cl $\text{Molar mass of NaCl}=23+35.5=58.5\text{g mol}^{-1}$ To convert the concentration from moles per liter to grams per liter (strength), multiply the molar concentration ( $C$ ) by the molar mass: $\text{Strength}(\text{g L}^{-1})=\text{Molar concentration} \times \text{Molar mass}$ $\text{Strength}=0.25\text{mol L}^{-1} \times 58.5\text{g mol}^{-1}$ $\text{Strength}=14.625\text{g L}^{-1}$ Rounding off to the nearest integer, we get $15$ . The strength of the sodium chloride solution is 15 $\text{g L}^{-1}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Osmotic pressure ( $\pi$ ) = $12\text{atm}$

Temperature ( $T$ ) = $300\text{K}$

Gas constant ( $R$ ) = $0.08\text{L atm K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$

Sodium chloride (NaCl) is an electrolyte that breaks into ions in an aqueous solution:

$\text{NaCl} \rightarrow \text{Na}^{+}+\text{Cl}^{-}$

Since it is given to assume complete dissociation, one unit of NaCl produces 2 ions.

Therefore, the van 't Hoff factor, $i=2$ .

According to the formula for osmotic pressure:

$\pi=iCRT$

Substitute the given values into the equation:

$12=2 \times C \times 0.08 \times 300$

$12=2 \times 24 \times C$

$12=48 \times C$

$C=\frac{12}{48}$

$C=0.25\text{mol L}^{-1}$

Molar mass of NaCl = Molar mass of Na + Molar mass of Cl

$\text{Molar mass of NaCl}=23+35.5=58.5\text{g mol}^{-1}$

To convert the concentration from moles per liter to grams per liter (strength), multiply the molar concentration ( $C$ ) by the molar mass:

$\text{Strength}(\text{g L}^{-1})=\text{Molar concentration} \times \text{Molar mass}$

$\text{Strength}=0.25\text{mol L}^{-1} \times 58.5\text{g mol}^{-1}$

$\text{Strength}=14.625\text{g L}^{-1}$

Rounding off to the nearest integer, we get $15$ .

The strength of the sodium chloride solution is 15 $\text{g L}^{-1}$ .

questions.question_text: Solution A is prepared by dissolving 1 g of a protein (molar mass = 50,000 g mol -1 ) in 0.5 L of water at 300 K. Its osmotic pressure is $x$ bar. Solution B is made by dissolving 2 g of the same protein in 1 L of water at 300 K. Osmotic pressure of solution B is $y$ bar. Entire solution of A is mixed with entire solution of B at the same temperature. The osmotic pressure of resultant solution is $z$ bar. $x$ , $y$ and $z$ respectively are: (R = 0.083 L bar mol -1 K -1 )
questions.question_html:
Solution A is prepared by dissolving 1 g of a protein (molar mass = 50,000 g mol-1) in 0.5 L of water at 300 K. Its osmotic pressure is $x$ bar. Solution B is made by dissolving 2 g of the same protein in 1 L of water at 300 K. Osmotic pressure of solution B is $y$ bar. Entire solution of A is mixed with entire solution of B at the same temperature. The osmotic pressure of resultant solution is $z$ bar. $x$ , $y$ and $z$ respectively are:
(R = 0.083 L bar mol-1 K-1)
questions.explanation_text: For osmotic pressure, we use the NCERT relation: $\pi=CRT=\frac{n}{V}RT$ where $\pi$ = osmotic pressure $n$ = number of moles of solute $V$ = volume of solution $R=0.083\text{L bar mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ $T=300\text{K}$ Protein molar mass is: $M=50000\text{g mol}^{-1}$ Now solve each part. For solution A Mass of protein $=1\text{g}$ Moles of protein: $n_{A}=\frac{1}{50000}=2 \times 10^{-5}\text{mol}$ Volume: $V_{A}=0.5\text{L}$ So concentration: $C_{A}=\frac{2 \times 10^{-5}}{0.5}=4 \times 10^{-5}\text{mol L}^{-1}$ Hence osmotic pressure: $x=\pi_{A}=C_{A}RT$ $x=(4 \times 10^{-5})(0.083)(300)$ First calculate: $0.083 \times 300=24.9$ So, $x=4 \times 10^{-5} \times 24.9=9.96 \times 10^{-4}\text{bar}$ For solution B Mass of protein $=2\text{g}$ Moles: $n_{B}=\frac{2}{50000}=4 \times 10^{-5}\text{mol}$ Volume: $V_{B}=1\text{L}$ Concentration: $C_{B}=\frac{4 \times 10^{-5}}{1}=4 \times 10^{-5}\text{mol L}^{-1}$ Thus, $y=\pi_{B}=C_{B}RT$ $y=(4 \times 10^{-5})(0.083)(300)$ $y=9.96 \times 10^{-4}\text{bar}$ After mixing A and B Total moles of protein: $n_{\text{total}}=2 \times 10^{-5}+4 \times 10^{-5}=6 \times 10^{-5}\text{mol}$ Total volume: $V_{\text{total}}=0.5+1=1.5\text{L}$ Concentration after mixing: $C_{\text{mix}}=\frac{6 \times 10^{-5}}{1.5}=4 \times 10^{-5}\text{mol L}^{-1}$ Again, $z=\pi_{\text{mix}}=C_{\text{mix}}RT$ $z=(4 \times 10^{-5})(0.083)(300)=9.96 \times 10^{-4}\text{bar}$ So, $x=9.96 \times 10^{-4}\text{bar},y=9.96 \times 10^{-4}\text{bar},z=9.96 \times 10^{-4}\text{bar}$ Therefore, the correct option is: $\text{Option A}$
questions.explanation_html:
For osmotic pressure, we use the NCERT relation:

$\pi=CRT=\frac{n}{V}RT$

where

  • $\pi$ = osmotic pressure

  • $n$ = number of moles of solute

  • $V$ = volume of solution

  • $R=0.083\text{L bar mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$

  • $T=300\text{K}$

Protein molar mass is:

$M=50000\text{g mol}^{-1}$

Now solve each part.

For solution A

Mass of protein $=1\text{g}$

Moles of protein:

$n_{A}=\frac{1}{50000}=2 \times 10^{-5}\text{mol}$

Volume:

$V_{A}=0.5\text{L}$

So concentration:

$C_{A}=\frac{2 \times 10^{-5}}{0.5}=4 \times 10^{-5}\text{mol L}^{-1}$

Hence osmotic pressure:

$x=\pi_{A}=C_{A}RT$

$x=(4 \times 10^{-5})(0.083)(300)$

First calculate:

$0.083 \times 300=24.9$

So,

$x=4 \times 10^{-5} \times 24.9=9.96 \times 10^{-4}\text{bar}$

For solution B

Mass of protein $=2\text{g}$

Moles:

$n_{B}=\frac{2}{50000}=4 \times 10^{-5}\text{mol}$

Volume:

$V_{B}=1\text{L}$

Concentration:

$C_{B}=\frac{4 \times 10^{-5}}{1}=4 \times 10^{-5}\text{mol L}^{-1}$

Thus,

$y=\pi_{B}=C_{B}RT$

$y=(4 \times 10^{-5})(0.083)(300)$

$y=9.96 \times 10^{-4}\text{bar}$

After mixing A and B

Total moles of protein:

$n_{\text{total}}=2 \times 10^{-5}+4 \times 10^{-5}=6 \times 10^{-5}\text{mol}$

Total volume:

$V_{\text{total}}=0.5+1=1.5\text{L}$

Concentration after mixing:

$C_{\text{mix}}=\frac{6 \times 10^{-5}}{1.5}=4 \times 10^{-5}\text{mol L}^{-1}$

Again,

$z=\pi_{\text{mix}}=C_{\text{mix}}RT$

$z=(4 \times 10^{-5})(0.083)(300)=9.96 \times 10^{-4}\text{bar}$

So,

$x=9.96 \times 10^{-4}\text{bar},y=9.96 \times 10^{-4}\text{bar},z=9.96 \times 10^{-4}\text{bar}$

Therefore, the correct option is:

$\text{Option A}$

When 1 g of $PQ$ is dissolved in 50 g of solvent ' $A^{'},\Delta T_{b}$ was 1.176 K while when 1 g of $PQ_{2}$ is dissolved in 50 g of solvent ' $A^{'},\Delta T_{b}$ was 0.689 K . ( $K_{b}$ of ' $A^{'}=5Kkgmol^{-1}$ ). The molar masses of elements P and Q (in $gmol^{-1}$ ) respectively, are :
questions.question_html: Elements P and Q form two types of non-volatile, non-ionizable compounds PQ and $PQ_{2}$ . When 1 g of $PQ$ is dissolved in 50 g of solvent ' $A^{'},\Delta T_{b}$ was 1.176 K while when 1 g of $PQ_{2}$ is dissolved in 50 g of solvent ' $A^{'},\Delta T_{b}$ was 0.689 K . ( $K_{b}$ of ' $A^{'}=5Kkgmol^{-1}$ ). The molar masses of elements P and Q (in $gmol^{-1}$ ) respectively, are :
questions.explanation_text: For a non-volatile, non-ionizable solute, $\Delta T_{b}=K_{b}m$ and $m=\frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{kg of solvent}}$ Given: mass of solvent $=50\text{g}=0.05\text{kg}$ , mass of solute $=1\text{g}$ . So for any solute of molar mass $M$ , $m=\frac{\frac{1}{M}}{0.05}=\frac{1}{0.05M}=\frac{20}{M}$ Hence, $\Delta T_{b}=K_{b} \cdot \frac{20}{M}=5 \cdot \frac{20}{M}=\frac{100}{M}$ So, $M=\frac{100}{\Delta T_{b}}$ 1) For $PQ$ $M(PQ)=\frac{100}{1.176} \approx 85.03 \approx 85$ Let molar masses of elements be $P=x$ and $Q=y$ : $x+y=85...(1)$ 2) For $PQ_{2}$ $M(PQ_{2})=\frac{100}{0.689} \approx 145.14 \approx 145$ So, $x+2y=145...(2)$ Subtract (1) from (2): $(x+2y)-(x+y)=145-85 \Rightarrow y=60$ Then from (1): $x+60=85 \Rightarrow x=25$ Therefore, molar masses are: $P=25,Q=60$ Correct option: A (25, 60)
questions.explanation_html:
For a non-volatile, non-ionizable solute,

$\Delta T_{b}=K_{b}m$

and

$m=\frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{kg of solvent}}$

Given: mass of solvent $=50\text{g}=0.05\text{kg}$ , mass of solute $=1\text{g}$ .

So for any solute of molar mass $M$ ,

$m=\frac{\frac{1}{M}}{0.05}=\frac{1}{0.05M}=\frac{20}{M}$

Hence,

$\Delta T_{b}=K_{b} \cdot \frac{20}{M}=5 \cdot \frac{20}{M}=\frac{100}{M}$

So,

$M=\frac{100}{\Delta T_{b}}$

1) For $PQ$

$M(PQ)=\frac{100}{1.176} \approx 85.03 \approx 85$

Let molar masses of elements be $P=x$ and $Q=y$ :

$x+y=85...(1)$

2) For $PQ_{2}$

$M(PQ_{2})=\frac{100}{0.689} \approx 145.14 \approx 145$

So,

$x+2y=145...(2)$

Subtract (1) from (2):

$(x+2y)-(x+y)=145-85 \Rightarrow y=60$

Then from (1):

$x+60=85 \Rightarrow x=25$

Therefore, molar masses are:

$P=25,Q=60$

Correct option: A (25, 60)

questions.question_text: 19.5 g of fluoro acetic acid (molar mass = 78 g mol −1 ) is dissolved in 500 g of water at 298 K. The depression in the freezing point of water was 1 ∘ C. What is $K_{a}$ of fluoro acetic acid? (For water, $K_{f}=1.86$ K kg mol −1 ). Assume molarity and molality to have same values.
questions.question_html:
19.5 g of fluoro acetic acid (molar mass = 78 g mol−1) is dissolved in 500 g of water at 298 K. The depression in the freezing point of water was 1∘C. What is $K_{a}$ of fluoro acetic acid?

(For water, $K_{f}=1.86$ K kg mol−1). Assume molarity and molality to have same values.
questions.explanation_text: Given: Mass of fluoroacetic acid $=19.5\text{g}$ Molar mass $=78\text{g mol}^{-1}$ Mass of water $=500\text{g}=0.5\text{kg}$ Depression in freezing point, $\Delta T_{f}=1^{\circ}\text{C}=1\text{K}$ $K_{f}=1.86\text{K kg mol}^{-1}$ We have to find $K_{a}$ of fluoroacetic acid. First, calculate the number of moles of acid: $n=\frac{19.5}{78}=0.25\text{mol}$ Now, molality of the solution: $m=\frac{0.25}{0.5}=0.5\text{mol kg}^{-1}$ For an electrolyte, $\Delta T_{f}=iK_{f}m$ So, $1=i \times 1.86 \times 0.5$ $1=i \times 0.93$ $i=\frac{1}{0.93} \approx 1.075$ Fluoroacetic acid is a weak monoprotic acid: $\text{HA} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^{+}+\text{A}^{-}$ If degree of dissociation is $\alpha$ , then for this type of acid: $i=1+\alpha$ Therefore, $\alpha=i-1=1.075-1=0.075$ Now use Ostwald’s dilution law: $K_{a}=\frac{C\alpha^{2}}{1-\alpha}$ Given in the question, assume molarity and molality are same, so $C=0.5$ Thus, $K_{a}=\frac{0.5 \times (0.075)^{2}}{1-0.075}$ $=\frac{0.5 \times 0.005625}{0.925}$ $=\frac{0.0028125}{0.925} \approx 3.04 \times 10^{-3}$ So, $K_{a} \approx 3 \times 10^{-3}$ Hence, the correct option is: $3 \times 10^{-3}$ Option D.
questions.explanation_html:
Given:

  • Mass of fluoroacetic acid $=19.5\text{g}$

  • Molar mass $=78\text{g mol}^{-1}$

  • Mass of water $=500\text{g}=0.5\text{kg}$

  • Depression in freezing point, $\Delta T_{f}=1^{\circ}\text{C}=1\text{K}$

  • $K_{f}=1.86\text{K kg mol}^{-1}$

We have to find $K_{a}$ of fluoroacetic acid.

First, calculate the number of moles of acid:

$n=\frac{19.5}{78}=0.25\text{mol}$

Now, molality of the solution:

$m=\frac{0.25}{0.5}=0.5\text{mol kg}^{-1}$

For an electrolyte,

$\Delta T_{f}=iK_{f}m$

So,

$1=i \times 1.86 \times 0.5$

$1=i \times 0.93$

$i=\frac{1}{0.93} \approx 1.075$

Fluoroacetic acid is a weak monoprotic acid:

$\text{HA} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^{+}+\text{A}^{-}$

If degree of dissociation is $\alpha$ , then for this type of acid:

$i=1+\alpha$

Therefore,

$\alpha=i-1=1.075-1=0.075$

Now use Ostwald’s dilution law:

$K_{a}=\frac{C\alpha^{2}}{1-\alpha}$

Given in the question, assume molarity and molality are same, so

$C=0.5$

Thus,

$K_{a}=\frac{0.5 \times (0.075)^{2}}{1-0.075}$

$=\frac{0.5 \times 0.005625}{0.925}$

$=\frac{0.0028125}{0.925} \approx 3.04 \times 10^{-3}$

So,

$K_{a} \approx 3 \times 10^{-3}$

Hence, the correct option is:

$3 \times 10^{-3}$

Option D.

questions.question_text: Two liquids A and B form an ideal solution at temperature T K . At T K , the vapour pressures of pure A and B are 55 and $15kNm^{-2}$ respectively. What is the mole fraction of A in solution of A and B in equilibrium with a vapour in which the mole fraction of A is 0.8?
questions.question_html: Two liquids A and B form an ideal solution at temperature T K . At T K , the vapour pressures of pure A and B are 55 and $15kNm^{-2}$ respectively. What is the mole fraction of A in solution of A and B in equilibrium with a vapour in which the mole fraction of A is 0.8?
questions.explanation_text: For an ideal solution, Raoult’s law applies: $p_{A}=x_{A}P_{A}^{∗},p_{B}=x_{B}P_{B}^{∗}$ Total pressure: $P=p_{A}+p_{B}=55x_{A}+15(1-x_{A})=55x_{A}+15-15x_{A}=40x_{A}+15$ Vapour-phase mole fraction (Dalton’s law): $y_{A}=\frac{p_{A}}{P}=\frac{55x_{A}}{40x_{A}+15}=0.8$ Solve: $55x_{A}=0.8(40x_{A}+15)=32x_{A}+12$ $23x_{A}=12 \Rightarrow x_{A}=\frac{12}{23}=0.5217$ Answer: 0.5217 (Option A)
questions.explanation_html:
For an ideal solution, Raoult’s law applies:

$p_{A}=x_{A}P_{A}^{∗},p_{B}=x_{B}P_{B}^{∗}$

Total pressure:

$P=p_{A}+p_{B}=55x_{A}+15(1-x_{A})=55x_{A}+15-15x_{A}=40x_{A}+15$

Vapour-phase mole fraction (Dalton’s law):

$y_{A}=\frac{p_{A}}{P}=\frac{55x_{A}}{40x_{A}+15}=0.8$

Solve:

$55x_{A}=0.8(40x_{A}+15)=32x_{A}+12$

$23x_{A}=12 \Rightarrow x_{A}=\frac{12}{23}=0.5217$

Answer: 0.5217 (Option A)

questions.question_html:
At $T(K),100g$ of $98%H_{2}SO_{4}(w/w)$ aqueous solution is mixed with 100 g of $49%H_{2}SO_{4}(w/w)$ aqueous solution. What is the mole fraction of $H_{2}SO_{4}$ in the resultant solution?

(Given : Atomic mass $H=1u;S=32u;O=16u$ ).

(Assume that temperature after mixing remains constant)
questions.explanation_text: Total mass of $H_{2}SO_{4}$ in the mixture: $=(100 \times \frac{98}{100})+(100 \times \frac{49}{100})=147gm$ Here, the first solution gives $98g$ of $H_{2}SO_{4}$ and the second gives $49g$ of $H_{2}SO_{4}$ , so total is $147g$ . Total mass of solution after mixing $=100+100=200g$ . So, total mass of $H_{2}O$ in the mixture: Total weight of $H_{2}O=200-147=53gm$ Moles of $H_{2}SO_{4}=\frac{147}{98}$ (since molar mass of $H_{2}SO_{4}$ is $98gmol^{-1}$ ). Moles of $H_{2}O=\frac{53}{18}$ (since molar mass of $H_{2}O$ is $18gmol^{-1}$ ). Now, mole fraction of $H_{2}SO_{4}$ is: Mole fraction of $H_{2}SO_{4}=\frac{\frac{147}{98}}{(\frac{147}{98}+\frac{53}{18})}=0.337$
questions.explanation_html:
Total mass of $H_{2}SO_{4}$ in the mixture:

$=(100 \times \frac{98}{100})+(100 \times \frac{49}{100})=147gm$

Here, the first solution gives $98g$ of $H_{2}SO_{4}$ and the second gives $49g$ of $H_{2}SO_{4}$ , so total is $147g$ .

Total mass of solution after mixing $=100+100=200g$ .

So, total mass of $H_{2}O$ in the mixture:

Total weight of $H_{2}O=200-147=53gm$

Moles of $H_{2}SO_{4}=\frac{147}{98}$ (since molar mass of $H_{2}SO_{4}$ is $98gmol^{-1}$ ).

Moles of $H_{2}O=\frac{53}{18}$ (since molar mass of $H_{2}O$ is $18gmol^{-1}$ ).

Now, mole fraction of $H_{2}SO_{4}$ is:

Mole fraction of $H_{2}SO_{4}=\frac{\frac{147}{98}}{(\frac{147}{98}+\frac{53}{18})}=0.337$

questions.question_text: When 0.25 moles of a non-volatile, non-ionizable solute was dissolved in 1 mole of a solvent the vapor pressure of solution was $x%$ of vapor pressure of pure solvent. What is $x%$ ?
questions.question_html: When 0.25 moles of a non-volatile, non-ionizable solute was dissolved in 1 mole of a solvent the vapor pressure of solution was $x%$ of vapor pressure of pure solvent. What is $x%$ ?
questions.explanation_text: Let the mole fraction of the solvent be $x_{1}$ and that of the solute be $x_{2}$ . Given: Moles of solute $n_{2}=0.25$ Moles of solvent $n_{1}=1$ $x_{1}=\frac{n_{1}}{n_{1}+n_{2}}=\frac{1}{1+0.25}=\frac{1}{1.25}=0.8$ $x_{2}=1-x_{1}=1-0.8=0.2$ For a non-volatile solute, the vapor pressure of the solution is given by: $P_{\text{solution}}=x_{1}P^{0}$ where $P^{0}$ is the vapor pressure of the pure solvent. $\frac{P_{\text{solution}}}{P^{0}} \times 100=x_{1} \times 100=0.8 \times 100=80%$ Final Answer: $x=80%$ Option D: 80%
questions.explanation_html:
Let the mole fraction of the solvent be $x_{1}$ and that of the solute be $x_{2}$ .

Given:

Moles of solute $n_{2}=0.25$

Moles of solvent $n_{1}=1$

$x_{1}=\frac{n_{1}}{n_{1}+n_{2}}=\frac{1}{1+0.25}=\frac{1}{1.25}=0.8$

$x_{2}=1-x_{1}=1-0.8=0.2$

For a non-volatile solute, the vapor pressure of the solution is given by:

$P_{\text{solution}}=x_{1}P^{0}$

where $P^{0}$ is the vapor pressure of the pure solvent.

$\frac{P_{\text{solution}}}{P^{0}} \times 100=x_{1} \times 100=0.8 \times 100=80%$

Final Answer:

$x=80%$

Option D: 80%

questions.explanation_text: Liquid A and B form an ideal solution. The vapor pressures of pure liquids A and B are 350 mm Hg and 750 mm Hg, respectively, at the same temperature. Here, $x_{A}$ and $x_{B}$ represent the mole fractions of A and B in the solution, and $y_{A}$ and $y_{B}$ are their mole fractions in the vapor phase. Let’s begin by comparing the vapor pressures: $P_{A}^{o}<P_{B}^{o}$ $\frac{P_{A}^{o}}{P_{B}^{o}}<1$ The relationship between the mole fractions in the vapor phase and the solution can be expressed as: $\frac{y_{A}}{y_{B}}=\frac{P_{A}^{o}}{P_{B}^{o}} \cdot \frac{x_{A}}{x_{B}}$ Since $\frac{P_{A}^{o}}{P_{B}^{o}}<1$ , it follows that: $\frac{\frac{y_{A}}{y_{B}}}{\frac{x_{A}}{x_{B}}}<1$ Which implies: $\frac{y_{A}}{y_{B}}<\frac{x_{A}}{x_{B}}$ This indicates that the mole fraction ratio of A to B in the vapor phase is less than that in the solution.
questions.explanation_html:
Liquid A and B form an ideal solution. The vapor pressures of pure liquids A and B are 350 mm Hg and 750 mm Hg, respectively, at the same temperature. Here, $x_{A}$ and $x_{B}$ represent the mole fractions of A and B in the solution, and $y_{A}$ and $y_{B}$ are their mole fractions in the vapor phase.

Let’s begin by comparing the vapor pressures:

$P_{A}^{o}<P_{B}^{o}$

$\frac{P_{A}^{o}}{P_{B}^{o}}<1$

The relationship between the mole fractions in the vapor phase and the solution can be expressed as:

$\frac{y_{A}}{y_{B}}=\frac{P_{A}^{o}}{P_{B}^{o}} \cdot \frac{x_{A}}{x_{B}}$

Since $\frac{P_{A}^{o}}{P_{B}^{o}}<1$ , it follows that:

$\frac{\frac{y_{A}}{y_{B}}}{\frac{x_{A}}{x_{B}}}<1$

Which implies:

$\frac{y_{A}}{y_{B}}<\frac{x_{A}}{x_{B}}$

This indicates that the mole fraction ratio of A to B in the vapor phase is less than that in the solution.

2 moles each of ethylene glycol and glucose are dissolved in 500 g of water. The boiling point of the resulting solution is:
(Given : Ebullioscopic constant of water $=0.52Kkgmol^{-1}$ )
questions.question_html: 2 moles each of ethylene glycol and glucose are dissolved in 500 g of water. The boiling point of the resulting solution is: (Given : Ebullioscopic constant of water $=0.52Kkgmol^{-1}$ )
questions.explanation_text: Boiling Point Elevation Formula : $\Delta T_{b}=i_{1} \cdot m_{1} \cdot K_{b}+i_{2} \cdot m_{2} \cdot K_{b}$ where: $i_{1}$ and $i_{2}$ are the van't Hoff factors for ethylene glycol and glucose, respectively (both are 1 since they do not dissociate in solution). $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ are the molalities of ethylene glycol and glucose, respectively. $K_{b}$ is the ebullioscopic constant of water ( $0.52\text{K kg mol}^{-1}$ ). Calculate Molality : Each solute has 2 moles dissolved in 500 grams of water ( $0.5\text{kg}$ ): $m_{1}=\frac{2\text{moles}}{0.5\text{kg}}=4\text{mol kg}^{-1}$ $m_{2}=\frac{2\text{moles}}{0.5\text{kg}}=4\text{mol kg}^{-1}$ Substitute into the Formula : $\Delta T_{b}=1 \cdot 4 \cdot 0.52+1 \cdot 4 \cdot 0.52=4.16$ Determine Boiling Point of Solution : The normal boiling point of water is $373.16\text{K}$ . Add the boiling point elevation to the normal boiling point: $T_{b}(\text{solution})=373.16+4.16=377.3\text{K}$ Thus, the boiling point of the resulting solution is $377.3\text{K}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Boiling Point Elevation Formula:

$\Delta T_{b}=i_{1} \cdot m_{1} \cdot K_{b}+i_{2} \cdot m_{2} \cdot K_{b}$

where:

$i_{1}$ and $i_{2}$ are the van't Hoff factors for ethylene glycol and glucose, respectively (both are 1 since they do not dissociate in solution).

$m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ are the molalities of ethylene glycol and glucose, respectively.

$K_{b}$ is the ebullioscopic constant of water ( $0.52\text{K kg mol}^{-1}$ ).

Calculate Molality:

Each solute has 2 moles dissolved in 500 grams of water ( $0.5\text{kg}$ ):

$m_{1}=\frac{2\text{moles}}{0.5\text{kg}}=4\text{mol kg}^{-1}$

$m_{2}=\frac{2\text{moles}}{0.5\text{kg}}=4\text{mol kg}^{-1}$

Substitute into the Formula:

$\Delta T_{b}=1 \cdot 4 \cdot 0.52+1 \cdot 4 \cdot 0.52=4.16$

Determine Boiling Point of Solution:

The normal boiling point of water is $373.16\text{K}$ .

Add the boiling point elevation to the normal boiling point:

$T_{b}(\text{solution})=373.16+4.16=377.3\text{K}$

Thus, the boiling point of the resulting solution is $377.3\text{K}$ .

questions.question_text: What is the freezing point depression constant of a solvent, 50 g of which contain 1 g non volatile solute (molar mass $256gmol^{-1}$ ) and the decrease in freezing point is 0.40 K ?
questions.question_html: What is the freezing point depression constant of a solvent, 50 g of which contain 1 g non volatile solute (molar mass $256gmol^{-1}$ ) and the decrease in freezing point is 0.40 K ?
questions.explanation_text: To find the freezing point depression constant ( $K_{f}$ ) of the solvent, we use the formula for freezing point depression: $\Delta T_{f}=K_{f} \cdot m$ Given: The decrease in freezing point $\Delta T_{f}$ is 0.40 K. The mass of the solute is 1 g and its molar mass is 256 g/mol. The mass of the solvent is 50 g (or 0.050 kg). First, calculate the molality ( $m$ ): Molality is defined as the moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. Calculate moles of solute: $\text{Moles of solute}=\frac{1\text{g}}{256\text{g/mol}}=\frac{1}{256}\text{mol}$ Calculate molality ( $m$ ): $m=\frac{\frac{1}{256}\text{mol}}{0.050\text{kg}}=\frac{1}{256 \times 0.050}\text{mol/kg}$ Now, substitute into the formula to find $K_{f}$ : $0.4=K_{f} \cdot \frac{1}{256 \times 0.050}$ Solving for $K_{f}$ : $K_{f}=0.4 \cdot 256 \times 0.050=5.12\text{K kg/mol}$ Thus, the freezing point depression constant of the solvent is $5.12\text{K kg/mol}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
To find the freezing point depression constant ( $K_{f}$ ) of the solvent, we use the formula for freezing point depression:

$\Delta T_{f}=K_{f} \cdot m$

Given:

The decrease in freezing point $\Delta T_{f}$ is 0.40 K.

The mass of the solute is 1 g and its molar mass is 256 g/mol.

The mass of the solvent is 50 g (or 0.050 kg).

First, calculate the molality ( $m$ ):

Molality is defined as the moles of solute per kilogram of solvent.

Calculate moles of solute:

$\text{Moles of solute}=\frac{1\text{g}}{256\text{g/mol}}=\frac{1}{256}\text{mol}$

Calculate molality ( $m$ ):

$m=\frac{\frac{1}{256}\text{mol}}{0.050\text{kg}}=\frac{1}{256 \times 0.050}\text{mol/kg}$

Now, substitute into the formula to find $K_{f}$ :

$0.4=K_{f} \cdot \frac{1}{256 \times 0.050}$

Solving for $K_{f}$ :

$K_{f}=0.4 \cdot 256 \times 0.050=5.12\text{K kg/mol}$

Thus, the freezing point depression constant of the solvent is $5.12\text{K kg/mol}$ .

questions.question_text: If A 2 B is 30% ionised in an aqueous solution, then the value of van't Hoff factor (i) is _______ × 10 −1 .
questions.question_html: If A2B is 30% ionised in an aqueous solution, then the value of van't Hoff factor (i) is _______ × 10−1.
questions.explanation_text: Percent ionisation of $A_{2}B=30%$ The dissociation of $A_{2}B$ in aqueous solution can be represented as $A_{2}B \rightarrow 2A^{+}+B^{2-}$ 1 mole of $A_{2}B$ produces 2 moles of $A^{+}$ and 1 mole of $B^{2-}$ ions. The total number of moles of ions produced (n) from the dissociation is $n=2+1=3$ The degree of dissociation given that $A_{2}B$ is 30% ionised, the degree of dissociation $(\lambda)$ or degree of ionisation $\lambda=\frac{30}{100}=0.3$ Van't Hoff factor ( $i$ ) can be calculated using the formula, $i=1+(n-1)\lambda$ Substitute the values of $n$ and $\lambda$ as, $i=1+(3-1) \times 0.3$ $=1+2 \times 0.3$ $=1+0.6$ $=1.6$ $=16 \times 10^{-1}$
questions.explanation_html:
Percent ionisation of $A_{2}B=30%$

The dissociation of $A_{2}B$ in aqueous solution can be represented as

$A_{2}B \rightarrow 2A^{+}+B^{2-}$

1 mole of $A_{2}B$ produces 2 moles of $A^{+}$ and 1 mole of $B^{2-}$ ions.

The total number of moles of ions produced (n) from the dissociation is

$n=2+1=3$

The degree of dissociation given that $A_{2}B$ is 30% ionised, the degree of dissociation $(\lambda)$ or degree of ionisation

$\lambda=\frac{30}{100}=0.3$

Van't Hoff factor ( $i$ ) can be calculated using the formula,

$i=1+(n-1)\lambda$

Substitute the values of $n$ and $\lambda$ as,

$i=1+(3-1) \times 0.3$

$=1+2 \times 0.3$

$=1+0.6$

$=1.6$

$=16 \times 10^{-1}$

Thus, the volume change upon mixing, denoted as $\Delta V_{\text{mix}}$ , is zero. (D) Solution of acetic acid in benzene: In this mixture, acetic acid tends to dimerize. questions.explanation_text: Freezing Point Depression: $\Delta T_{f}=i \times K_{f} \times m$ Given: $\Delta T_{f}=0.2\text{°C},K_{f}=1.8\text{K kg mol}^{-1},m=0.1\text{m}$ Substituting the given values: $0.2=i \times 1.8 \times 0.1$ Solving for $i$ : $i=\frac{0.2}{1.8 \times 0.1}=\frac{20}{18}=\frac{10}{9}$ Degree of Dissociation ( $\alpha$ ): For the reaction $HA \rightleftharpoons H^{+}+A^{-}$ : $i=1+\alpha$ Given $i=\frac{10}{9}$ : $\frac{10}{9}=1+\alpha$ $\alpha=\frac{1}{9}$ Dissociation Constant ( $K_{eq}$ ): $K_{eq}=\frac{[H^{+}][A^{-}]}{[HA]}$ At equilibrium: $[H^{+}]=[A^{-}]=\alpha \times C=\frac{1}{9} \times 0.1$ $[HA]=0.1 \times (1-\alpha)=0.1 \times (1-\frac{1}{9})$ Substituting these into $K_{eq}$ : $K_{eq}=\frac{(0.1 \times \frac{1}{9})^{2}}{0.1 \times (1-\frac{1}{9})}$ Simplifying: $K_{eq}=\frac{0.1 \times (\frac{1}{81})}{0.1 \times \frac{8}{9}}=\frac{1}{720}$ Therefore: $K_{eq}=1.38 \times 10^{-3}$
questions.explanation_html:
Freezing Point Depression:

$\Delta T_{f}=i \times K_{f} \times m$

Given:

$\Delta T_{f}=0.2\text{°C},K_{f}=1.8\text{K kg mol}^{-1},m=0.1\text{m}$

Substituting the given values:

$0.2=i \times 1.8 \times 0.1$

Solving for $i$ :

$i=\frac{0.2}{1.8 \times 0.1}=\frac{20}{18}=\frac{10}{9}$

Degree of Dissociation ( $\alpha$ ):

For the reaction $HA \rightleftharpoons H^{+}+A^{-}$ :

$i=1+\alpha$

Given $i=\frac{10}{9}$ :

$\frac{10}{9}=1+\alpha$

$\alpha=\frac{1}{9}$

Dissociation Constant ( $K_{eq}$ ):

$K_{eq}=\frac{[H^{+}][A^{-}]}{[HA]}$

At equilibrium:

$[H^{+}]=[A^{-}]=\alpha \times C=\frac{1}{9} \times 0.1$

$[HA]=0.1 \times (1-\alpha)=0.1 \times (1-\frac{1}{9})$

Substituting these into $K_{eq}$ :

$K_{eq}=\frac{(0.1 \times \frac{1}{9})^{2}}{0.1 \times (1-\frac{1}{9})}$

Simplifying:

$K_{eq}=\frac{0.1 \times (\frac{1}{81})}{0.1 \times \frac{8}{9}}=\frac{1}{720}$

Therefore:

$K_{eq}=1.38 \times 10^{-3}$

questions.explanation_text: When $x$ grams of NaCl are added to water in a beaker and the temperature is increased from $1^{\circ}C$ to $25^{\circ}C$ , the molarity of the solution changes due to the volumetric changes of water. Temperature from $1^{\circ}C$ to $4^{\circ}C$ : Water is densest at $4^{\circ}C$ . As the temperature increases from $1^{\circ}C$ to $4^{\circ}C$ , the water volume decreases due to increased density. This decrease in volume results in an increase in molarity because molarity is inversely proportional to the solution's volume. Temperature from $4^{\circ}C$ to $25^{\circ}C$ : Beyond $4^{\circ}C$ , water expands with an increase in temperature. Therefore, as temperature rises to $25^{\circ}C$ , the volume of the water increases. The dilution leads to a decrease in molarity, since molarity is inversely proportional to volume. Thus, the molarity first increases as temperature rises to $4^{\circ}C$ , but then decreases as it continues to $25^{\circ}C$ . The graphical representation of this relationship would exhibit an initial increase in molarity, followed by a decrease, correlating with changes in the volume of water due to temperature variations.

questions.explanation_text: Mass of $Ax_{2}=1.24g$ (solute) Molarmass of $AX_{2}=124gmol^{-1}$ Mass of water $=1kg$ (solvent.) Boiling point of water $=100^{\circ}C$ Boiling point of water after adding solute $AX_{2}=100.0156^{\circ}C$ Mass of $AY_{2}=25.4g$ (solute) Molarmass of $AY_{2}=250gmol^{-1}$ Mass of water $=2kg$ (Solvent) Boiling point of water $\mp 100^{\circ}C$ Boiling point of water after adding solute $Ay_{2}=100.0260^{\circ}C$ $K_{b}(H_{2}O)=0.52Kkgmol^{-1}=0.520^{\circ}Ckgmol^{-1}$ The ionisation of $Ax_{2}$ and $AY_{2}$ can be determined by calculating Van't Hoff factor. The phenomenon given in the question is elevation in boiling point. The boiling point of solvent increases when another compound (solute) is added to it. Relation: $\Delta T_{b}=K_{b} \cdot i \cdot m$ $\Delta T_{b}=T_{b}-T_{b}^{0}$ $\Delta T_{b} \rightarrow$ Boiling point elevation $T_{b} \rightarrow$ Boiling point of solution (solvent + solute) $T_{b}^{0} \rightarrow$ Boiling point of solvent $K_{b} \rightarrow$ Molal elevation constant $i \rightarrow$ Van't Hoff factor $m \rightarrow \text{Molality}=\frac{\text{Number of moles}}{kg\text{of solvent}},\text{Moles}=\frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Molarmass}}$ For $AX_{2}$ and $AY_{2}$ (solute), Van't Hoff factor represents how many particles a solute dissociates into when dissolved in a solvent (water). For non-electrolytes, $i=1$ $\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} & AX_{2}: \\ & \text{Moles}=\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{molarmass}}=\frac{1.249}{124gmol^{-1}}=0.01mol \\ & \text{Molality}=\frac{\text{Moles}}{k_{g}\text{of solvent}}=\frac{0.01mol}{1kg}=0.01molkg^{-1} \\ & \Delta T_{b}=K_{b} \times i \times m \\ & i=\frac{\Delta T_{b}}{k_{b} \times m} \\ & =\frac{T_{b}-T_{b}^{0}}{K_{b} \times m} \end{aligned} \\ & \text{Substitute values as.,} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} i & =\frac{(100.0156^{\circ}C-100^{\circ}C)}{0.52^{\circ}Ckgmol^{-1} \times 0.01molkg^{-1}} \\ & =\frac{0.0156^{\circ}C}{0.52 \times 0.01^{\circ}C}=3 \end{aligned}$ $i=3$ means, there are 3 particles in solution after $AX_{2}$ dissolved in water. $Ax_{2} \rightarrow 1A^{+}+2X^{-}(1+2=3)$ $\begin{aligned} & Ax_{2}\text{is completely ionised.} \\ & AY_{2}: \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} \text{Moles} & =\frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Molarmass}}=\frac{25.4g}{250gmol}=0.1016mol \\ \text{Molality} & =\frac{\text{Moles}}{kgof^{-1}\text{solvent}}=\frac{0.1016mol}{2kg}=0.050.8molkg^{-1} \\ \Delta T_{b} & =k_{b} \times l^{2} \times m \\ i & =\frac{\Delta T_{b}}{k_{b} \times m} \\ & =\frac{T_{b}-T_{b}^{0}}{k_{b} \times m} \end{aligned} \\ & \text{Substitute values as,} \end{aligned}$ $i=\frac{(100.0260^{\circ}C-100^{\circ}C)}{0.52^{\circ}Ckgmol^{-1} \times 0.0508molkg^{-1}}$ $=\frac{0.0260^{\circ}C}{0.52 \times 0.0508^{\circ}C}$ $=0.98$ $\approx 1$ $i=1$ means $AY_{2}$ is completely unionised. $Ay_{2}$ not give ionised particles when dissolved in water. So, $AX_{2}$ is completely ionised and $AY_{2}$ is completely unionised. Answer: Option 4) $Ax_{2}$ is fully ionised, $AY_{2}$ is completely unionised.

The ionisation of $Ax_{2}$ and $AY_{2}$ can be determined by calculating Van't Hoff factor.

The phenomenon given in the question is elevation in boiling point. The boiling point of solvent increases when another compound (solute) is added to it.

Relation: $\Delta T_{b}=K_{b} \cdot i \cdot m$

$\Delta T_{b}=T_{b}-T_{b}^{0}$

$\Delta T_{b} \rightarrow$ Boiling point elevation

$T_{b} \rightarrow$ Boiling point of solution (solvent + solute)

$i \rightarrow$ Van't Hoff factor

$m \rightarrow \text{Molality}=\frac{\text{Number of moles}}{kg\text{of solvent}},\text{Moles}=\frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Molarmass}}$

For $AX_{2}$ and $AY_{2}$ (solute), Van't Hoff factor represents how many particles a solute dissociates into when dissolved in a solvent (water).

For non-electrolytes, $i=1$

$\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} & AX_{2}: \\ & \text{Moles}=\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{molarmass}}=\frac{1.249}{124gmol^{-1}}=0.01mol \\ & \text{Molality}=\frac{\text{Moles}}{k_{g}\text{of solvent}}=\frac{0.01mol}{1kg}=0.01molkg^{-1} \\ & \Delta T_{b}=K_{b} \times i \times m \\ & i=\frac{\Delta T_{b}}{k_{b} \times m} \\ & =\frac{T_{b}-T_{b}^{0}}{K_{b} \times m} \end{aligned} \\ & \text{Substitute values as.,} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} i & =\frac{(100.0156^{\circ}C-100^{\circ}C)}{0.52^{\circ}Ckgmol^{-1} \times 0.01molkg^{-1}} \\ & =\frac{0.0156^{\circ}C}{0.52 \times 0.01^{\circ}C}=3 \end{aligned}$

$i=3$ means, there are 3 particles in solution after $AX_{2}$ dissolved in water.

$Ax_{2} \rightarrow 1A^{+}+2X^{-}(1+2=3)$

$\begin{aligned} & Ax_{2}\text{is completely ionised.} \\ & AY_{2}: \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} \text{Moles} & =\frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Molarmass}}=\frac{25.4g}{250gmol}=0.1016mol \\ \text{Molality} & =\frac{\text{Moles}}{kgof^{-1}\text{solvent}}=\frac{0.1016mol}{2kg}=0.050.8molkg^{-1} \\ \Delta T_{b} & =k_{b} \times l^{2} \times m \\ i & =\frac{\Delta T_{b}}{k_{b} \times m} \\ & =\frac{T_{b}-T_{b}^{0}}{k_{b} \times m} \end{aligned} \\ & \text{Substitute values as,} \end{aligned}$

$i=\frac{(100.0260^{\circ}C-100^{\circ}C)}{0.52^{\circ}Ckgmol^{-1} \times 0.0508molkg^{-1}}$

$=\frac{0.0260^{\circ}C}{0.52 \times 0.0508^{\circ}C}$

$=0.98$

$\approx 1$

$i=1$ means $AY_{2}$ is completely unionised.

$Ay_{2}$ not give ionised particles when dissolved in water.

So, $AX_{2}$ is completely ionised and $AY_{2}$ is completely unionised.

Answer: Option 4) $Ax_{2}$ is fully ionised, $AY_{2}$ is completely unionised.

questions.question_text: When a non-volatile solute is added to the solvent, the vapour pressure of the solvent decreases by 10 mm of Hg . The mole fraction of the solute in the solution is 0.2 . What would be the mole fraction of the solvent if decrease in vapour pressure is 20 mm of Hg ?
questions.question_html: When a non-volatile solute is added to the solvent, the vapour pressure of the solvent decreases by 10 mm of Hg . The mole fraction of the solute in the solution is 0.2 . What would be the mole fraction of the solvent if decrease in vapour pressure is 20 mm of Hg ?
questions.explanation_text: When a non-volatile solute is added to a solvent, it causes the vapour pressure of the solvent to decrease. In this scenario, when the vapour pressure decreases by 10 mm of Hg, the mole fraction of the solute in the solution is 0.2. By understanding the relationship between vapour pressure change and mole fraction, we see that: The change in vapour pressure ( $P^{\circ}-P$ ) is directly proportional to the mole fraction of the solute ( $X_{\text{solute}}$ ). Therefore, if a 10 mm of Hg decrease corresponds to a mole fraction of 0.2, then a 20 mm of Hg decrease would correspond to a mole fraction of 0.4. To find the mole fraction of the solvent ( $X_{\text{solvent}}$ ), we use the formula: $X_{\text{solvent}}=1-X_{\text{solute}}$ Substituting the value we found: $X_{\text{solvent}}=1-0.4=0.6$ Thus, when the vapour pressure decreases by 20 mm of Hg, the mole fraction of the solvent is 0.6.

When a non-volatile solute is added to a solvent, it causes the vapour pressure of the solvent to decrease. In this scenario, when the vapour pressure decreases by 10 mm of Hg, the mole fraction of the solute in the solution is 0.2.

By understanding the relationship between vapour pressure change and mole fraction, we see that:

The change in vapour pressure ( $P^{\circ}-P$ ) is directly proportional to the mole fraction of the solute ( $X_{\text{solute}}$ ).

Therefore, if a 10 mm of Hg decrease corresponds to a mole fraction of 0.2, then a 20 mm of Hg decrease would correspond to a mole fraction of 0.4.

To find the mole fraction of the solvent ( $X_{\text{solvent}}$ ), we use the formula:

$X_{\text{solvent}}=1-X_{\text{solute}}$

Substituting the value we found:

$X_{\text{solvent}}=1-0.4=0.6$

Thus, when the vapour pressure decreases by 20 mm of Hg, the mole fraction of the solvent is 0.6.

questions.explanation_text: Given: 1 mole of volatile liquid A 3 moles of volatile liquid B Vapor pressure of pure A, $P_{A}^{o}=200$ mm Hg Vapor pressure of the solution, $P_{S}=500$ mm Hg We apply Raoult's law, which states: $P_{S}=P_{A}^{o} \cdot X_{A}+P_{B}^{o} \cdot X_{B}$ Where: $X_{A}$ is the mole fraction of A $X_{B}$ is the mole fraction of B $P_{B}^{o}$ is the vapor pressure of pure liquid B Calculate the mole fractions: $X_{A}=\frac{1}{1+3}=\frac{1}{4}$ $X_{B}=\frac{3}{1+3}=\frac{3}{4}$ Plug these into the equation: $500=200 \times \frac{1}{4}+P_{B}^{o} \times \frac{3}{4}$ Simplifying: $500=50+\frac{3}{4}P_{B}^{o}$ Subtract 50 from both sides: $450=\frac{3}{4}P_{B}^{o}$ Multiply both sides by $\frac{4}{3}$ to solve for $P_{B}^{o}$ : $P_{B}^{o}=600\text{mm Hg}$ Since $P_{A}^{o}<P_{B}^{o}$ , liquid A is the least volatile component. In conclusion: The vapor pressure of pure B, $P_{B}^{o}$ , is 600 mm Hg. The least volatile component is A.
questions.explanation_html:
Given:

1 mole of volatile liquid A

3 moles of volatile liquid B

Vapor pressure of pure A, $P_{A}^{o}=200$ mm Hg

Vapor pressure of the solution, $P_{S}=500$ mm Hg

We apply Raoult's law, which states:

$P_{S}=P_{A}^{o} \cdot X_{A}+P_{B}^{o} \cdot X_{B}$

Where:

$X_{A}$ is the mole fraction of A

$X_{B}$ is the mole fraction of B

$P_{B}^{o}$ is the vapor pressure of pure liquid B

Calculate the mole fractions:

$X_{A}=\frac{1}{1+3}=\frac{1}{4}$

$X_{B}=\frac{3}{1+3}=\frac{3}{4}$

Plug these into the equation:

$500=200 \times \frac{1}{4}+P_{B}^{o} \times \frac{3}{4}$

Simplifying:

$500=50+\frac{3}{4}P_{B}^{o}$

Subtract 50 from both sides:

$450=\frac{3}{4}P_{B}^{o}$

Multiply both sides by $\frac{4}{3}$ to solve for $P_{B}^{o}$ :

$P_{B}^{o}=600\text{mm Hg}$

Since $P_{A}^{o}<P_{B}^{o}$ , liquid A is the least volatile component.

In conclusion:

The vapor pressure of pure B, $P_{B}^{o}$ , is 600 mm Hg.

The least volatile component is A.

questions.question_text: Consider a binary solution of two volatile liquid components 1 and $2.x_{1}$ and $y_{1}$ are the mole fractions of component 1 in liquid and vapour phase, respectively. The slope and intercept of the linear plot of $\frac{1}{x_{1}}$ vs $\frac{1}{y_{1}}$ are given respectively as :
questions.question_html: Consider a binary solution of two volatile liquid components 1 and $2.x_{1}$ and $y_{1}$ are the mole fractions of component 1 in liquid and vapour phase, respectively. The slope and intercept of the linear plot of $\frac{1}{x_{1}}$ vs $\frac{1}{y_{1}}$ are given respectively as :
questions.explanation_text: For a binary solution of two volatile liquid components labeled 1 and 2, let $x_{1}$ and $y_{1}$ represent the mole fractions of component 1 in the liquid and vapor phases, respectively. The linear relationship between the inverse of these mole fractions is plotted as $\frac{1}{x_{1}}$ versus $\frac{1}{y_{1}}$ . To derive the slope and intercept of this linear plot, consider the following calculations: Using Raoult's Law for a Liquid Solution: For a liquid solution with volatile components 1 and 2: $P_{1}=P_{T} \cdot y_{1}=P_{1}^{o} \cdot x_{1}$ Therefore: $\frac{P_{T}}{x_{1}}=\frac{P_{1}^{o}}{y_{1}}$ Rearranging the Equation: By substituting and rearranging, we have: $\frac{P_{2}^{o}+x_{1}(P_{1}^{o}-P_{2}^{o})}{x_{1}}=\frac{P_{1}^{o}}{y_{1}}$ Simplifying further: $\frac{P_{2}^{o}}{x_{1}}+(P_{1}^{o}-P_{2}^{o})=\frac{P_{1}^{o}}{y_{1}}$ Expressing $\frac{1}{x_{1}}$ : Solving for $\frac{1}{x_{1}}$ , we obtain: $\frac{1}{x_{1}}=(\frac{P_{1}^{o}}{P_{2}^{o}})(\frac{1}{y_{1}})+(\frac{P_{2}^{o}-P_{1}^{o}}{P_{2}^{o}})$ Determining the Slope and Intercept: The slope of the line is: $\text{Slope}=\frac{P_{1}^{o}}{P_{2}^{o}}$ The intercept of the line is: $\text{Intercept}=\frac{P_{2}^{o}-P_{1}^{o}}{P_{2}^{o}}$ In summary, for the plot of $\frac{1}{x_{1}}$ against $\frac{1}{y_{1}}$ , the slope is $\frac{P_{1}^{o}}{P_{2}^{o}}$ and the intercept is $\frac{P_{2}^{o}-P_{1}^{o}}{P_{2}^{o}}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
For a binary solution of two volatile liquid components labeled 1 and 2, let $x_{1}$ and $y_{1}$ represent the mole fractions of component 1 in the liquid and vapor phases, respectively. The linear relationship between the inverse of these mole fractions is plotted as $\frac{1}{x_{1}}$ versus $\frac{1}{y_{1}}$ .

To derive the slope and intercept of this linear plot, consider the following calculations:

Using Raoult's Law for a Liquid Solution:

For a liquid solution with volatile components 1 and 2:

$P_{1}=P_{T} \cdot y_{1}=P_{1}^{o} \cdot x_{1}$

Therefore:

$\frac{P_{T}}{x_{1}}=\frac{P_{1}^{o}}{y_{1}}$

Rearranging the Equation:

By substituting and rearranging, we have:

$\frac{P_{2}^{o}+x_{1}(P_{1}^{o}-P_{2}^{o})}{x_{1}}=\frac{P_{1}^{o}}{y_{1}}$

Simplifying further:

$\frac{P_{2}^{o}}{x_{1}}+(P_{1}^{o}-P_{2}^{o})=\frac{P_{1}^{o}}{y_{1}}$

Expressing $\frac{1}{x_{1}}$ :

Solving for $\frac{1}{x_{1}}$ , we obtain:

$\frac{1}{x_{1}}=(\frac{P_{1}^{o}}{P_{2}^{o}})(\frac{1}{y_{1}})+(\frac{P_{2}^{o}-P_{1}^{o}}{P_{2}^{o}})$

Determining the Slope and Intercept:

The slope of the line is:

$\text{Slope}=\frac{P_{1}^{o}}{P_{2}^{o}}$

The intercept of the line is:

$\text{Intercept}=\frac{P_{2}^{o}-P_{1}^{o}}{P_{2}^{o}}$

In summary, for the plot of $\frac{1}{x_{1}}$ against $\frac{1}{y_{1}}$ , the slope is $\frac{P_{1}^{o}}{P_{2}^{o}}$ and the intercept is $\frac{P_{2}^{o}-P_{1}^{o}}{P_{2}^{o}}$ .

questions.question_html:
When 1 g each of compounds AB and $AB_{2}$ are dissolved in 15 g of water separately, they increased the boiling point of water by 2.7 K and 1.5 K respectively. The atomic mass of A (in $amu$ ) is____________ $\times 10^{-1}$ (Nearest integer)

(Given : Molal boiling point elevation constant is $0.5Kkgmol^{-1}$ )
questions.explanation_text: For AB $\begin{aligned} & \Delta T_{b}=2.7K \\ & 2.7=1 \times 0.5 \times m \\ & m=\frac{27}{5} \end{aligned}$ Let molar mass of $AB=x$ . So $\frac{1/x}{15} \times 1000=\frac{27}{5}$ $x=12.34$ For $AB_{2}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Delta T_{b}=1.5K \\ & 1.5=1 \times 0.5 \times m \\ & m=3 \end{aligned}$ Let molar mass of $AB_{2}=y$ So $\frac{1/y}{15} \times 1000=3$ $\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1000}{45} \\ & y=22.22 \end{aligned}$ Now let a and b be atomic masses of A and B respectively, then $\begin{aligned} & A+b=12.34\text{...... (i)} \\ & A+2b=22.22\text{...... (ii)} \\ & B=22.22-12.34=9.88 \end{aligned}$ Now $a=12.34-9.88=2.46$ $=24.6 \times 10^{-1}=25 \times 10^{-1}$
questions.explanation_html:
For AB

$\begin{aligned} & \Delta T_{b}=2.7K \\ & 2.7=1 \times 0.5 \times m \\ & m=\frac{27}{5} \end{aligned}$

Let molar mass of $AB=x$ .

So $\frac{1/x}{15} \times 1000=\frac{27}{5}$

$x=12.34$

For $AB_{2}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Delta T_{b}=1.5K \\ & 1.5=1 \times 0.5 \times m \\ & m=3 \end{aligned}$

Let molar mass of $AB_{2}=y$

So $\frac{1/y}{15} \times 1000=3$

$\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1000}{45} \\ & y=22.22 \end{aligned}$

Now let a and b be atomic masses of A and B respectively, then

$\begin{aligned} & A+b=12.34\text{...... (i)} \\ & A+2b=22.22\text{...... (ii)} \\ & B=22.22-12.34=9.88 \end{aligned}$

Now $a=12.34-9.88=2.46$

$=24.6 \times 10^{-1}=25 \times 10^{-1}$

If $5mL$ of acetic acid is dissolved in 1 litre water, the solution will freeze at $-x \times 10^{-2}^{\circ}C$ , provided pure water freezes at $0^{\circ}C$ . $x=$ _________. (Nearest integer) $\begin{aligned} \text{Given :} & (K_{f})_{\text{water}}=1.86Kkgmol-1 \\ & \text{density of acetic acid is}1.2gmol^{-1}\text{.} \\ & \text{molar mass of water}=18gmol^{-1}\text{.} \\ & \text{molar mass of acetic acid=}60gmol^{-1}\text{.} \\ & \text{density of water}=1gcm^{-3} \end{aligned}$ Acetic acid dissociates as $CH_{3}COOH \rightleftharpoons CH_{3}COO^{\circ}+H^{⊕}$

Considering acetic acid dissociates in water, its dissociation constant is $6.25 \times 10^{-5}$ . If $5mL$ of acetic acid is dissolved in 1 litre water, the solution will freeze at $-x \times 10^{-2}^{\circ}C$ , provided pure water freezes at $0^{\circ}C$ .

questions.explanation_text: To solve the problem, we'll calculate the freezing point depression of the acetic acid solution in water. Calculating Moles of Acetic Acid : Given volume of acetic acid: $5\text{mL}$ Density of acetic acid: $1.2\text{g/mL}$ Molar mass of acetic acid: $60\text{g/mol}$ $\text{Mass of acetic acid}=\text{Volume} \times \text{Density}=5\text{mL} \times 1.2\text{g/mL}=6\text{g}$ $\text{Moles of acetic acid}=\frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Molar mass}}=\frac{6\text{g}}{60\text{g/mol}}=0.1\text{mol}$ Calculating Molality : Volume of water: $1\text{L}$ Density of water: $1\text{g/cm}^{3} \Rightarrow 1\text{kg/L}$ Hence, mass of water = $1\text{kg}$ $\text{Molality (m)}=\frac{\text{Moles of solute}}{\text{Mass of solvent (kg)}}=\frac{0.1\text{mol}}{1\text{kg}}=0.1\text{mol/kg}$ Degree of Dissociation ( $\alpha$ ) : Dissociation constant ( $K_{a}$ ) of acetic acid: $6.25 \times 10^{-5}$ $\alpha=\sqrt{\frac{K_{a}}{C}}=\sqrt{\frac{6.25 \times 10^{-5}}{0.1}}=\sqrt{6.25 \times 10^{-4}}=25 \times 10^{-3}=0.025$ Van't Hoff factor (i) : Acetic acid partially dissociates into 2 ions (CH $_{3}$ COO $^{-}$ and H $^{+}$ ) $i=1+(\text{number of ions produced}-1) \times \alpha=1+(2-1) \times 0.025=1+0.025=1.025$ Freezing Point Depression ( $\Delta T_{f}$ ) : Freezing point depression constant ( $K_{f}$ ) for water: $1.86\text{K kg/mol}$ $\Delta T_{f}=i \times K_{f} \times \text{Molality}=1.025 \times 1.86 \times 0.1=0.19065\text{K}$ Final Freezing Point : Pure water freezes at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ $\text{Freezing point of solution}=0^{\circ}\text{C}-0.19065^{\circ}\text{C}=-0.19065^{\circ}\text{C}$ Here, $-x \times 10^{-2}^{\circ}\text{C}$ is given. Therefore, $x=19$ (nearest integer). So, the final answer is: $x=19$
questions.explanation_html:
To solve the problem, we'll calculate the freezing point depression of the acetic acid solution in water.

  1. Calculating Moles of Acetic Acid:
  • Given volume of acetic acid: $5\text{mL}$

  • Density of acetic acid: $1.2\text{g/mL}$

  • Molar mass of acetic acid: $60\text{g/mol}$

$\text{Mass of acetic acid}=\text{Volume} \times \text{Density}=5\text{mL} \times 1.2\text{g/mL}=6\text{g}$

$\text{Moles of acetic acid}=\frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Molar mass}}=\frac{6\text{g}}{60\text{g/mol}}=0.1\text{mol}$

  1. Calculating Molality:
  • Volume of water: $1\text{L}$

  • Density of water: $1\text{g/cm}^{3} \Rightarrow 1\text{kg/L}$

  • Hence, mass of water = $1\text{kg}$

$\text{Molality (m)}=\frac{\text{Moles of solute}}{\text{Mass of solvent (kg)}}=\frac{0.1\text{mol}}{1\text{kg}}=0.1\text{mol/kg}$

  1. Degree of Dissociation ( $\alpha$ ):
  • Dissociation constant ( $K_{a}$ ) of acetic acid: $6.25 \times 10^{-5}$

$\alpha=\sqrt{\frac{K_{a}}{C}}=\sqrt{\frac{6.25 \times 10^{-5}}{0.1}}=\sqrt{6.25 \times 10^{-4}}=25 \times 10^{-3}=0.025$

  1. Van't Hoff factor (i):
  • Acetic acid partially dissociates into 2 ions (CH $_{3}$ COO $^{-}$ and H $^{+}$ )

$i=1+(\text{number of ions produced}-1) \times \alpha=1+(2-1) \times 0.025=1+0.025=1.025$

  1. Freezing Point Depression ( $\Delta T_{f}$ ):
  • Freezing point depression constant ( $K_{f}$ ) for water: $1.86\text{K kg/mol}$

$\Delta T_{f}=i \times K_{f} \times \text{Molality}=1.025 \times 1.86 \times 0.1=0.19065\text{K}$

  1. Final Freezing Point:
  • Pure water freezes at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$

$\text{Freezing point of solution}=0^{\circ}\text{C}-0.19065^{\circ}\text{C}=-0.19065^{\circ}\text{C}$

Here, $-x \times 10^{-2}^{\circ}\text{C}$ is given. Therefore, $x=19$ (nearest integer).

So, the final answer is:

$x=19$

questions.question_text: Mass of ethylene glycol (antifreeze) to be added to $18.6kg$ of water to protect the freezing point at $-24^{\circ}C$ is ________ $kg$ (Molar mass in $gmol^{-1}$ for ethylene glycol $62,K_{f}$ of water $=1.86K$ $kgmol^{-1}$ )
questions.question_html: Mass of ethylene glycol (antifreeze) to be added to $18.6kg$ of water to protect the freezing point at $-24^{\circ}C$ is ________ $kg$ (Molar mass in $gmol^{-1}$ for ethylene glycol $62,K_{f}$ of water $=1.86K$ $kgmol^{-1}$ )
questions.explanation_text: To determine the mass of ethylene glycol (antifreeze) needed to lower the freezing point of water to $-24^{\circ}C$ , we can use the freezing point depression equation, which is a colligative property given by: $\Delta T_{f}=i \cdot K_{f} \cdot m$ where: $\Delta T_{f}$ is the depression in the freezing point. $i$ is the van't Hoff factor, which is the number of particles the solute splits into in solution. For ethylene glycol, which does not dissociate in solution, $i=1$ . $K_{f}$ is the cryoscopic constant (freezing point depression constant) of water, which is given as $1.86Kkgmol^{-1}$ . $m$ is the molality of the solution. However, molality is defined as the number of moles of solute per kilogram of solvent, so we first need to find the molality that corresponds to the desired freezing point depression: $\Delta T_{f}=-24^{\circ}C-(0^{\circ}C)=-24^{\circ}C$ Now, we can solve for $m$ : $m=\frac{\Delta T_{f}}{i \cdot K_{f}}$ Substituting the given values: $m=\frac{-24^{\circ}C}{1 \cdot 1.86Kkgmol^{-1}}$ Note that $C$ and $K$ are interchangeable when calculating changes in temperature. Now, we can compute the molality: $m=\frac{-24}{1.86}$ Next, we calculate the molality of the ethylene glycol: $m \approx -12.903molkg^{-1}$ Keep in mind that molality is always positive, but the negative sign indicates the direction of the temperature change. Since we're calculating the amount needed, we can consider it as 12.903 moles per kilogram of water. Now we calculate the moles of ethylene glycol required for $18.6kg$ of water: $\text{moles of ethylene glycol}=m \cdot \text{mass of water (in kg)}$ $\text{moles of ethylene glycol}=12.903molkg^{-1} \cdot 18.6kg$ $\text{moles of ethylene glycol} \approx 240.0158mol$ Next, we find the mass of ethylene glycol needed using its molar mass: $\text{mass of ethylene glycol}=\text{moles of ethylene glycol} \cdot \text{molar mass of ethylene glycol}$ Given the molar mass of ethylene glycol is $62gmol^{-1}$ , we then convert it to $kgmol^{-1}$ by dividing by 1000: $\text{molar mass of ethylene glycol}=0.062kgmol^{-1}$ Now we can calculate the mass: $\text{mass of ethylene glycol}=240.0158mol \cdot 0.062kgmol^{-1}$ $\text{mass of ethylene glycol} \approx 14.88098kg$ Therefore, approximately $14.881kg$ of ethylene glycol needs to be added to $18.6kg$ of water to lower the freezing point to $-24^{\circ}C$ .
questions.explanation_html:
To determine the mass of ethylene glycol (antifreeze) needed to lower the freezing point of water to $-24^{\circ}C$ , we can use the freezing point depression equation, which is a colligative property given by:

$\Delta T_{f}=i \cdot K_{f} \cdot m$

where:

  • $\Delta T_{f}$ is the depression in the freezing point.
  • $i$ is the van't Hoff factor, which is the number of particles the solute splits into in solution. For ethylene glycol, which does not dissociate in solution, $i=1$ .
  • $K_{f}$ is the cryoscopic constant (freezing point depression constant) of water, which is given as $1.86Kkgmol^{-1}$ .
  • $m$ is the molality of the solution.

However, molality is defined as the number of moles of solute per kilogram of solvent, so we first need to find the molality that corresponds to the desired freezing point depression:

$\Delta T_{f}=-24^{\circ}C-(0^{\circ}C)=-24^{\circ}C$

Now, we can solve for $m$ :

$m=\frac{\Delta T_{f}}{i \cdot K_{f}}$

Substituting the given values:

$m=\frac{-24^{\circ}C}{1 \cdot 1.86Kkgmol^{-1}}$

Note that $C$ and $K$ are interchangeable when calculating changes in temperature. Now, we can compute the molality:

$m=\frac{-24}{1.86}$

Next, we calculate the molality of the ethylene glycol:

$m \approx -12.903molkg^{-1}$

Keep in mind that molality is always positive, but the negative sign indicates the direction of the temperature change. Since we're calculating the amount needed, we can consider it as 12.903 moles per kilogram of water.

Now we calculate the moles of ethylene glycol required for $18.6kg$ of water:

$\text{moles of ethylene glycol}=m \cdot \text{mass of water (in kg)}$ $\text{moles of ethylene glycol}=12.903molkg^{-1} \cdot 18.6kg$ $\text{moles of ethylene glycol} \approx 240.0158mol$

Next, we find the mass of ethylene glycol needed using its molar mass:

$\text{mass of ethylene glycol}=\text{moles of ethylene glycol} \cdot \text{molar mass of ethylene glycol}$

Given the molar mass of ethylene glycol is $62gmol^{-1}$ , we then convert it to $kgmol^{-1}$ by dividing by 1000:

$\text{molar mass of ethylene glycol}=0.062kgmol^{-1}$

Now we can calculate the mass:

$\text{mass of ethylene glycol}=240.0158mol \cdot 0.062kgmol^{-1}$ $\text{mass of ethylene glycol} \approx 14.88098kg$

Therefore, approximately $14.881kg$ of ethylene glycol needs to be added to $18.6kg$ of water to lower the freezing point to $-24^{\circ}C$ .

questions.explanation_text: When a small quantity of naphthalene is added to benzene, the freezing point of benzene decreases. This phenomenon is due to the colligative property known as freezing point depression. The addition of a solute, such as naphthalene, disrupts the orderly arrangement of solvent molecules in the solid phase, thereby lowering the freezing point. Mathematically, the decrease in freezing point ( $\Delta T_{f}$ ) can be represented by the equation: $\Delta T_{f}=i \cdot K_{f} \cdot m$ where: $i$ is the van't Hoff factor (which is 1 for naphthalene as it does not dissociate in solution), $K_{f}$ is the cryoscopic constant of the solvent (benzene), $m$ is the molality of the solution. Thus, the correct option is: Option B: Decreases

questions.question_text: The vapor pressure of pure benzene and methyl benzene at $27^{\circ}C$ is given as 80 Torr and 24 Torr, respectively. The mole fraction of methyl benzene in vapor phase, in equilibrium with an equimolar mixture of those two liquids (ideal solution) at the same temperature is _________ $\times 10^{-2}$ (nearest integer)
questions.question_html: The vapor pressure of pure benzene and methyl benzene at $27^{\circ}C$ is given as 80 Torr and 24 Torr, respectively. The mole fraction of methyl benzene in vapor phase, in equilibrium with an equimolar mixture of those two liquids (ideal solution) at the same temperature is _________ $\times 10^{-2}$ (nearest integer)
questions.explanation_text: To find the mole fraction of methyl benzene in the vapor phase when it is in equilibrium with an equimolar (equal mole) mixture of benzene and methyl benzene at $27^{\circ}C$ , we can apply Raoult's law for an ideal solution. Given the vapor pressures of pure benzene and methyl benzene are 80 Torr and 24 Torr, respectively. Raoult's law states that the partial vapor pressure of a component in a solution is equal to the vapor pressure of the pure component multiplied by its mole fraction in the solution ( $P_{i}=P_{i}^{\circ}x_{i}$ ), where $P_{i}$ is the partial vapor pressure of the component $i$ , $P_{i}^{\circ}$ is the vapor pressure of the pure component $i$ , and $x_{i}$ is the mole fraction of the component $i$ in the solution. For an equimolar mixture of benzene and methyl benzene, the mole fractions of benzene ( $x_{b}$ ) and methyl benzene ( $x_{mb}$ ) in the liquid phase are both $0.5$ , because the mixture is equimolar. The total pressure of the mixture ( $P_{total}$ ) can be calculated using Raoult's law for each component and summing up the individual pressures: $P_{total}=P_{benzene}+P_{metℎylbenzene}$ $P_{total}=(P_{b}^{\circ}x_{b})+(P_{mb}^{\circ}x_{mb})$ Substituting the given values: $P_{total}=(80 \times 0.5)+(24 \times 0.5)$ $P_{total}=40+12=52\text{Torr}$ The mole fraction of methyl benzene in the vapor phase ( $y_{mb}$ ) can be calculated using Dalton's law, which states that the partial pressure of a component in a mixture is equal to the mole fraction of that component in the vapor phase times the total pressure of the mixture. The partial pressure of methyl benzene can be obtained from Raoult's law as we did earlier: $P_{metℎylbenzene}=P_{mb}^{\circ}x_{mb}=24 \times 0.5=12\text{Torr}$ Using Dalton's law: $y_{mb}=\frac{P_{metℎylbenzene}}{P_{total}}$ Substituting the values: $y_{mb}=\frac{12}{52}$ $y_{mb}=\frac{6}{26}$ $y_{mb}=\frac{3}{13}$ To express $y_{mb}$ as a percentage times $10^{-2}$ : $y_{mb}=(\frac{3}{13}) \times 100 \times 10^{-2}$ $y_{mb} \approx 23.08 \times 10^{-2}$ So, the mole fraction of methyl benzene in the vapor phase, in equilibrium with an equimolar mixture of those two liquids at $27^{\circ}C$ , is approximately $23 \times 10^{-2}$ (rounded to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation_html:
To find the mole fraction of methyl benzene in the vapor phase when it is in equilibrium with an equimolar (equal mole) mixture of benzene and methyl benzene at $27^{\circ}C$ , we can apply Raoult's law for an ideal solution. Given the vapor pressures of pure benzene and methyl benzene are 80 Torr and 24 Torr, respectively.

Raoult's law states that the partial vapor pressure of a component in a solution is equal to the vapor pressure of the pure component multiplied by its mole fraction in the solution ( $P_{i}=P_{i}^{\circ}x_{i}$ ), where $P_{i}$ is the partial vapor pressure of the component $i$ , $P_{i}^{\circ}$ is the vapor pressure of the pure component $i$ , and $x_{i}$ is the mole fraction of the component $i$ in the solution.

For an equimolar mixture of benzene and methyl benzene, the mole fractions of benzene ( $x_{b}$ ) and methyl benzene ( $x_{mb}$ ) in the liquid phase are both $0.5$ , because the mixture is equimolar.

The total pressure of the mixture ( $P_{total}$ ) can be calculated using Raoult's law for each component and summing up the individual pressures:

$P_{total}=P_{benzene}+P_{metℎylbenzene}$

$P_{total}=(P_{b}^{\circ}x_{b})+(P_{mb}^{\circ}x_{mb})$

Substituting the given values:

$P_{total}=(80 \times 0.5)+(24 \times 0.5)$

$P_{total}=40+12=52\text{Torr}$

The mole fraction of methyl benzene in the vapor phase ( $y_{mb}$ ) can be calculated using Dalton's law, which states that the partial pressure of a component in a mixture is equal to the mole fraction of that component in the vapor phase times the total pressure of the mixture.

The partial pressure of methyl benzene can be obtained from Raoult's law as we did earlier:

$P_{metℎylbenzene}=P_{mb}^{\circ}x_{mb}=24 \times 0.5=12\text{Torr}$

Using Dalton's law:

$y_{mb}=\frac{P_{metℎylbenzene}}{P_{total}}$

Substituting the values:

$y_{mb}=\frac{12}{52}$

$y_{mb}=\frac{6}{26}$

$y_{mb}=\frac{3}{13}$

To express $y_{mb}$ as a percentage times $10^{-2}$ :

$y_{mb}=(\frac{3}{13}) \times 100 \times 10^{-2}$

$y_{mb} \approx 23.08 \times 10^{-2}$

So, the mole fraction of methyl benzene in the vapor phase, in equilibrium with an equimolar mixture of those two liquids at $27^{\circ}C$ , is approximately $23 \times 10^{-2}$ (rounded to the nearest integer).

questions.explanation_text: An artificial cell contains a 0.2 M glucose solution within a semipermeable membrane. When this cell is placed in a 0.05 M NaCl solution at 300 K, we need to determine the osmotic pressure developed, expressed as × 10⁻¹ bar. Given: Ideal Gas Constant, R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ Assume complete dissociation of NaCl. Explanation The osmotic pressure ( $\pi$ ) is calculated using the formula: $\pi=(i_{1}C_{1}-i_{2}C_{2})RT$ where: $i_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ are the van 't Hoff factor and concentration for glucose. $i_{2}$ and $C_{2}$ are the van 't Hoff factor and concentration for NaCl. $R$ is the ideal gas constant. $T$ is the temperature in Kelvin. For glucose: $i_{1}=1$ (glucose does not dissociate) $C_{1}=0.2$ M For NaCl: $i_{2}=2$ (NaCl dissociates into two ions, Na⁺ and Cl⁻) $C_{2}=0.05$ M Plugging in the values: $\pi=(1 \times 0.2-2 \times 0.05) \times 0.083 \times 300$ Calculating: $\pi=(0.2-0.1) \times 0.083 \times 300$ $\pi=0.1 \times 0.083 \times 300$ $\pi=2.5\text{bar}$ Hence, the osmotic pressure developed is $25 \times 10^{-1}$ bar.
questions.explanation_html:
An artificial cell contains a 0.2 M glucose solution within a semipermeable membrane. When this cell is placed in a 0.05 M NaCl solution at 300 K, we need to determine the osmotic pressure developed, expressed as × 10⁻¹ bar.

Given:

Ideal Gas Constant, R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

Assume complete dissociation of NaCl.

Explanation

The osmotic pressure ( $\pi$ ) is calculated using the formula:

$\pi=(i_{1}C_{1}-i_{2}C_{2})RT$

where:

$i_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ are the van 't Hoff factor and concentration for glucose.

$i_{2}$ and $C_{2}$ are the van 't Hoff factor and concentration for NaCl.

$R$ is the ideal gas constant.

$T$ is the temperature in Kelvin.

For glucose:

$i_{1}=1$ (glucose does not dissociate)

$C_{1}=0.2$ M

For NaCl:

$i_{2}=2$ (NaCl dissociates into two ions, Na⁺ and Cl⁻)

$C_{2}=0.05$ M

Plugging in the values:

$\pi=(1 \times 0.2-2 \times 0.05) \times 0.083 \times 300$

Calculating:

$\pi=(0.2-0.1) \times 0.083 \times 300$

$\pi=0.1 \times 0.083 \times 300$

$\pi=2.5\text{bar}$

Hence, the osmotic pressure developed is $25 \times 10^{-1}$ bar.

questions.question_html: The osmotic pressure of a dilute solution is $7 \times 10^{5}Pa$ at $273K$ . Osmotic pressure of the same solution at $283K$ is _________ $\times 10^{4}Nm^{-2}$ .
questions.explanation_text: To calculate the osmotic pressure of the solution at the new temperature, we can use the formula: $\pi=\text{CRT}$ Since the concentration $C$ and the gas constant $R$ remain constant, the ratio of the osmotic pressures at two different temperatures is given by: $\frac{\pi_{1}}{\pi_{2}}=\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}$ Thus, we can express the osmotic pressure at the second temperature as: $\pi_{2}=\frac{\pi_{1} \cdot T_{2}}{T_{1}}$ Substituting the given values: $\pi_{2}=\frac{7 \times 10^{5} \times 283}{273}$ After calculation, this simplifies to: $\pi_{2}=72.56 \times 10^{4}\text{Nm}^{-2}$
questions.explanation_html:
To calculate the osmotic pressure of the solution at the new temperature, we can use the formula:

$\pi=\text{CRT}$

Since the concentration $C$ and the gas constant $R$ remain constant, the ratio of the osmotic pressures at two different temperatures is given by:

$\frac{\pi_{1}}{\pi_{2}}=\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}$

Thus, we can express the osmotic pressure at the second temperature as:

$\pi_{2}=\frac{\pi_{1} \cdot T_{2}}{T_{1}}$

Substituting the given values:

$\pi_{2}=\frac{7 \times 10^{5} \times 283}{273}$

After calculation, this simplifies to:

$\pi_{2}=72.56 \times 10^{4}\text{Nm}^{-2}$

questions.question_html: We have three aqueous solutions of $NaCl$ labelled as ' $A$ ', ' $B$ ' and ' $C$ ' with concentration $0.1M$ , $0.01M$ and $0.001M$ , respectively. The value of van 't Hoff factor(i) for these solutions will be in the order :
questions.explanation_text: Salt Values of i (for different conc. of a Salt) NaCl 0.1 M 0.01 M 0.001 M 1.87 1.94 1.94 The van 't Hoff factor (i) is used to describe the number of particles a solute formula unit produces in a solution. For an electrolyte like $NaCl$ , which dissociates completely in very dilute solutions, the theoretical value of $i$ is approximately 2, since $NaCl$ dissociates into $Na^{+}$ and $Cl^{-}$ ions. In real scenarios, as the concentration of the solution decreases (making the solution more dilute), the interaction between the ions decreases, allowing more complete dissociation. Therefore, for practical purposes, the van 't Hoff factor $i$ approaches its theoretical maximum value as concentration decreases. Thus, for $NaCl$ solutions of concentrations $0.1M$ , $0.01M$ , and $0.001M$ , the fact that $NaCl$ dissociates more completely in more dilute solutions implies that $i$ increases with decreasing concentration. Hence, the order of $i$ based on the concentration would be $i_{A}<i_{B}<i_{C}$ , as concentration $0.1M>0.01M>0.001M$ , respectively. Thus, option B correctly describes the order of the van 't Hoff factors for these solutions.
